Our Plank Firm review score: ★★★★User score: ★★★★½.

For a mattress to be considered a good option for anyone with back pain, it needs to perform well in three specific areas; pressure relief, temperature regulation, and edge support.

Recent findings suggest that in order to select only the beds that offer meaningful relief to people with a bad back, we've combed our test data to ensure each of the mattresses featured here have scored a minimum of 3.5 out of 5 in our pressure relief, temperature and edge support tests. Here's how the Helix Midnight Luxe, Saatva Rx, Plank Firm and Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Essential performed and compare across these crucial metrics:.

Pressure relief score (out of 5).

Temperature regulation: Reliable temperature regulation is an important feature of a mattress for back pain. Waking up hot and sweaty can lead to more movement (like kicking off the covers), which can cause further injury. Pressure relief: This is a term to describe how much cushioning there is along the touch points of the mattress. For example, for side sleepers, this will be your shoulders, hips and knees. For back sleepers, this will likely be your lumbar region and upper back and shoulders. Minimal pressure relief can lead to a build-up of pressure, which can exacerbate existing pain. Edge Support: This describes how sturdy a mattress is at its edges and corners. This is an important feature for any mattress, but especially those with back pain who may need to sit comfortably and safely before standing.

The Helix Midnight Luxe is superbly comfortable for side sleepers, and it's also an excellent choice for those with lower and upper back pain, as well as hip pain. As a luxury hotel-style hybrid, it is a premium mattress. However, a current 25% sale means you can buy a queen Midnight Luxe for $1,874 at Helix. The pillow top is crafted from high density foam which cushions the shoulders hips and knees, but also keeps the spine in healthy alignment while sleeping. This high density foam also works to gently cradle the lumbar region, which is the 'S' shape of your back. Underpinning this support are up to 1,000 individually wrapped coils that prevent the hips from sinking. Our lead tester, who has experienced recurrent lower back pain for the past decade, felt none of the pain she usually experiences while sleeping on the Luxe. Temperature wise, our test data mirrored our real life experience. It's a breathable bed with reliably sturdy edges for sitting on before standing.The Luxe is accredited by the American Chiropractic Association and is a great fit for aches and pains. However, those with more pronounced back pain have the option to upgrade to ErgoAlign. This is a layer of denser foam around the mid-section, bolstering support in this area. Luxe is a great option for side and back sleeper with back ache but for significant back pain, we recommend the Saatva Rx below.

The Saatva Rx is our top recommendation for those living with significant back or joint conditions, such as sciatica or arthritis. It's an ACA accredited specialist mattress, and it's priced accordingly (it's $3,214 for a queen at Saatva in this year's Saatva Black Friday sale). A large part of what sets the Rx apart from other back pain beds pain is its Therapeutic Support Core. This is made up of the brand’s proprietary Wave-Tech Foam and individually wrapped coils for support, cradling the spine in all sleep positions. Above that, a layer of micro-coils sandwiched between two slabs of high-density foam and a strip of gel-infused memory foam provides soothing support along the lumbar.Saatva rates the Rx as 'Supportive Plush' but our experience of sleeping on it was that it errs on the firmer side, making it a more comfortable choice for back and stomach sleepers. It's still comfy for side sleepers, but our lead tester — who has mild scoliosis — felt her spine was better supported when sleeping on her back. For general aches and pains, we recommend the (slightly cheaper) Saatva Classic Mattress instead, which does an excellent job of soothing mild back and hip pain.

It's a common misconception that people with back pain need a solid mattress. However, some people simply prefer the feel of a firm bed. And at 30% off for Black Friday, a queen Plank Firm is $1,025.50 at Plank, which is excellent value for money on this top rated firm mattress.The Plank Firm is a dual-sided all foam mattress rated as Firm on one side and Extra Firm on the other. It's been crafted from the inside out, where 6" of high density foam underpins the unyielding sleep surface. Regardless of how you flip it, make no mistake, this is a firm mattress. With its 2" top layer of comfort foam which provides cushioning around the touch points of the bed, the Firm side will have wider appeal. However, with just 0.75" slither of comfort foam, the Extra Firm side feels reassuringly solid for those who want to keep their spine in healthy alignment when sleeping on their stomach.It's accredited by the ACA and boasts superb motion isolation, which is good news for bed sharers. It's also nice and sturdy around the edge. However, with a score of 3.5 out of 5 for temperature control, it just scrapes through our benchmark of being temperature regulating enough for it to be considered a good choice for back pain. For hot sleepers, we recommend upgrading to the GlacioTex cooling layer.

In a mattress for back pain guide featuring ACA accredited beds with zoned lumbar support, you might be wondering why we have added the Essential to the mix, a mattress that at $489.30 for a queen at Brooklyn Bedding costs a fraction of the price and boasts none of those things.That's because, when combing our test data, it became apparent that the Essential performs well enough in crucial areas (temperature regulation, edge support and pressure relief) to make it a good choice for side sleepers looking for cushioning around their shoulders and hips, without sacrificing healthy spinal alignment. It's supportive enough for lighter weight back sleepers, but heavier bodies with need something sturdier to prevent their hips from sinking in this position. The Essential comes in 5 different heights ranging from 6"to 14" and we tested the 10". Increasing the height will likely mean increasing the support... and also the price. For a sturdier all foam mattress for back sleeping within a similar price range, we would opt for the Siena Signature. It scored 3.3 out of 5 for temperature regulation but is a fantastic budget friendly, firmer choice. For ACA accreditation, enhanced cooling and zoned lumbar support, we recommend the Brooklyn Bedding CopperFlex Pro Hybrid, a mid-range marvel coming in at under $1,000 for a queen in the Brooklyn Bedding mattress sales.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of owners. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the firm’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the company has also introduced new restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple revealed plans to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give consumers more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted upcoming job listings that offer a closer look at its looks to develop autonomous AI agents:.

In one, Apple said it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:.

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”.

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “strategy and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Sources indicate that today’s report on the upcoming job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring users to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the organization could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the new job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how swiftly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally released its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Bram Berkowitz – Nov 22, 2026 at 3:27PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Apple ›.

One of the most fascinating parts of Berkshire Hathaway's sprawling business is its roughly $360 billion equity portfolio, in which the organization invests the float generated by its insurance business in a wide range of stocks across sectors.

According to recent reports, in his more than six decades as CEO of Berkshire, Warren Buffett built one of the best investing track records in history. He has since passed the torch to latest CEO Greg Abel, a longtime Berkshire veteran and close confidant of Buffett, who looks to continue Buffett's remarkably concentrated approach to investing.

Industry observers note that to this day, just three stocks make up nearly 47% of Berkshire's portfolio. Perhaps even more amazing is that none of these three are traditional artificial intelligence hyperscalers.

Sources indicate that while Berkshire's investment moves are a strong starting point, investors should realize that Berkshire rarely explains its positions. Its filings arrive with a delay, so treat them as a starting point for your own research, not a shopping list.

In a recent development, greg Abel. Image source: Getty Images.

In a recent development, apple (AAPL -1.90%) is Berkshire's largest position by a wide margin. The roughly 228 million shares haven't changed in four straight quarterly filings, a notable pause after Buffett trimmed the stake for nearly two years.

Buffett, Abel, and the Berkshire team probably like Apple due to its loyal customer base of more than 2.5 billion active devices, high-margin Services revenue, and massive share repurchases over the past decade-plus that have significantly reduced Apple's outstanding shares, thereby increasing Berkshire's slice of profits.

Apple repurchased $24 billion of stock in its latest quarter, on top of a new $100 billion authorization announced in the spring.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Recent findings suggest that with a market capitalization above $5 trillion, Apple is now the largest stock in the world by market value. The results back it up: Fiscal 2026 revenue hit a record $478.8 billion, up 15%, and earnings per share rose 20% to $8.98. September-quarter iPhone revenue set a record, and services revenue also reached an all-time high of $31.6 billion.

Trading around 39 times trailing earnings, Apple stock isn't cheap. It has a new CEO, John Ternus, and shareholders are keen to ensure the manufacturer can keep producing innovative consumer tech products.

Apple is also in an enviable position: It's not investing hundreds of billions in data centers and therefore not experiencing challenges with free cash flow. Furthermore, Apple's leadership in consumer tech hardware, such as the iPhone, means it is likely to play a major role in delivering artificial intelligence to the public.

It has been revealed that berkshire has held American Express (AXP -3.02%) since the early 1990s and owns more than 22% of the manufacturer. Amex has a fantastic brand and business model that are difficult to replicate.

Amex is both a credit card issuer and a payments network, meaning it extends credit to consumers and businesses and facilitates transactions between customers and merchants.

When run well, the credit card business can generate strong returns on capital, and Amex caters to a more affluent customer base that is typically more resilient during recessions. Meanwhile, the payments business generates capital-light recurring fee revenue. In the third quarter, net card fee growth accelerated to 17% year over year.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

However, the stock has struggled this year, lagging the S&P 500 as investors worry about stablecoins and regulatory pressure on card economics. The business, however, is doing fine. Q3 revenue hit a record $20.1 billion, up 9%. Billed business rose 8% to $454 billion, and Amex raised its full-year earnings guidance.

Berkshire hasn't touched its Amex position since the 1990s, so Abel and the team clearly do not share current investor concerns.

In a recent development, coca-Cola (KO +0.94%) may be the most Buffett stock of all. Berkshire has owned it since 1988 and holds 400 million shares. With the quarterly dividend now $0.53 per share, those shares generate roughly $848 million in annual dividends. The manufacturer has raised its payout for 64 consecutive years.

It has been revealed that abel and his team likely value many of the attributes that have always made the iconic beverage organization attractive: global brands, pricing power, and steady cash flow. Management expects at least $13 billion in free cash flow this year.

The stock has been a big winner this year, as investors rotate somewhat out of artificial intelligence and tech and into the best-in-breed consumer staples stock.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

In Q3, unit case volume at the firm grew 5%, organic revenue rose 7%, and comparable earnings per share climbed 11%. After the strong run this year, Coca-Cola is no longer cheap, trading over 29 times forward earnings.

So while upside may be capped in the near term, Coca-Cola can generate solid long-term returns through the business cycle.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with new privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several new features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

And speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing customers to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing newly introduced tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful update, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and consumers on the public beta can now try out these upcoming features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar highlights how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.

According to recent reports, in the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.

In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also highlights how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) just made stock market history with its IPO.
  • In a recent development, at $91.6 billion, the company raised more cash in its debut than any company before it.
  • Industry observers note that the company had the misfortune of going public while the broader AI sector is crashing on fears surrounding Nvidia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jeremy Bowman – Nov 22, 2026 at 3:30PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›.

Anthropic (ANT -8.50%) just made stock market history with its IPO.

In a recent development, at $91.6 billion, the company raised more cash in its debut than any company before it. That would seem to be a bullish sign for the stock, but after an initial pop, Anthropic closed Friday trading just 7% above its IPO price, and at one point the stock was trading just five cents above the $83 listing price.

Industry observers note that the company had the misfortune of going public while the broader AI sector is crashing on fears surrounding Nvidia. Anthropic also has plenty of skeptics, who have called out risks like the $900 billion it has in purchase commitments, falling token prices, competition from cheaper models, and concerns about circular financing in the industry involving Nvidia.

Those risks are all valid, but the company has also reported revenue growth of 1,200% year-over-year through the first three quarters of the year, and it's already reached a revenue run rate of $68 billion. No company this young has ever been this big. Over the longer term, Anthropic sees its technology playing a role in everything from curing diseases to designing chips to making robots and beyond. In other words, it's a high-risk, high-reward stock.

Anthropic is in a fresh, rapidly evolving industry, and one of the most pressing questions for investors at this point is whether it has a sustainable competitive advantage.

It has been revealed that investors typically look for one of four types of competitive advantage. Those include:.

Industry observers note that anthropic clearly isn't the low-cost provider. It's a frontier AI lab running on state-of-the-art chips from Nvidia and others. Distillation models like DeepSeek's R1 are an example of low-cost providers in generative AI.

It has been revealed that anthropic's brand is getting stronger and becoming more of a competitive advantage. Claude, its core intelligence platform and chatbot, now rivals OpenAI's ChatGPT in recognition, and its other products like Claude Cowork and Claude Code have become well-known as well. Anthropic's brand helps attract new consumers and keep existing ones. If Anthropic's brand is recognized as the best AI, that gives it a competitive advantage.

Recent findings suggest that at an enterprise level, switching costs do apply to a product like Claude, as they do to the rest of the software industry. A business that's paid for hundreds or even thousands of Claude seats is going to face friction if it wants to switch to another provider. At the individual consumer level, switching costs are minimal.

Network effects do not really apply to AI, as it isn't used to connect with other consumers.

Of these four, brand seems like Anthropic's best opportunity to build a competitive advantage, much like Apple's in smartphones and consumer electronics.

In a recent development, technology on its own isn't generally considered a source of sustainable competitive advantage, especially in a rapidly evolving field like AI. Anthropic took the lead from OpenAI in part by introducing more capable models, but the race between the two companies continues, and Anthropic is not guaranteed to maintain its lead.

Technology can help build a competitive advantage when it's combined with patents or trade secrets, regulatory barriers to entry, or a strong brand, and it's clearly a major reason for Anthropic's meteoric growth.

Being the technology leader in an industry is a competitive advantage, but it's often not seen as sustainable.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Anthropic sees its competitive advantage stemming from the flywheel below, which highlights how its usage improves its models, similar to Google Search, and also drives more investment, which makes its models better.

Sources indicate that anthropic's flywheels. Image source: Anthropic.

What Anthropic describes here is more about how its business model creates a flywheel that makes it better, rather than a true competitive advantage.

For a market leader, however, this kind of flywheel can drive a competitive advantage, as it has for Google Search, which learns and improves from the way consumers use the product.

According to recent reports, I don't think it's correct to say that Anthropic doesn't have a competitive advantage, even though none of the four main ones strongly apply. I think the combination of its brand, technology, and the improvement flywheels constitutes an emerging competitive advantage that will be tested over the coming months and years.

If the company can continue to gain market share, that should be interpreted as a sign that its competitive advantage is getting stronger, which makes the stock much more likely to be a winner.

We'll learn more over the coming months as Anthropic's first earnings report comes out, and the AI boom responds to its biggest test yet in the stock market, but if Anthropic can build a sustainable competitive advantage, it could become the most valuable tech giant in the world.

WhatsApp is gradually rolling out an increase to its group chat limit, allowing up to 1,500 participants to join in, instead of the previous 1,024 cap. Here are the details.

While there are exceptions, there are generally two kinds of WhatsApp customers: those who hate group chats, and those who can’t seem to be in enough of them.

If you’re in the second category, you’re likely aware that WhatsApp has steadily increased the number of participants allowed in group chats over the years, jumping from 100 to 256 in 2016, then to 512 and, soon after, to 1,024 in 2022.

Now, as spotted by WABetaInfo, WhatsApp is once again expanding that limit, raising the maximum number of participants in a group chat to 1,500.

According to the website, the newly introduced limit is rolling out to owners on iOS and Android, though the rollout is gradual, meaning “not every account will see the higher limit immediately.”.

WhatsApp is automatically updating existing groups to support the upcoming limit. This means that admins do not need to take any action to unlock the higher capacity. As soon as the enhancement becomes available to their accounts, their groups will support up to 1500 members. As a result, the update lets admins add up to 476 new members to their existing groups.

This rollout comes as WhatsApp has been working to make group chats easier to manage. Just last month, the company unveiled four newly introduced features, including the ability to pin messages indefinitely, share status updates within groups, filter conversations by mentions and replies, and share recent message history with new members after they join.

#131160. Breaking: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3539 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.
  • At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.
  • It has been revealed that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Remedy Robotics is testing whether surgeons can operate from afar.

At Remedy Robotics, the N1 System’s prototype console [lower left] awaits its operator, with cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell and the surgical robot in an adjoining room.

It has been revealed that I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.

The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.

“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell notes. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death.

When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm Klok.

The screen indicates my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics manufacturer. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.”.

Industry observers note that for Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one. That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold.

It has been revealed that but can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.

As recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.

Industry observers note that in a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.

Recent findings suggest that yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right.

Recent findings suggest that the N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away. Christie Hemm Klok.

Recent findings suggest that if all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”.

It has been revealed that sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team indicated me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.

In a recent development, remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.

I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction.

This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.

Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.

Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.

In a recent development, about a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga states. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.”.

Sources indicate that dreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In Fresh York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.

But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.

Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campbell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm Klok.

In the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics organization XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.

“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.

Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.

Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot.

It has been revealed that after preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.

In a recent development, in 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy Robotics.

Recent findings suggest that absent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.

Industry observers note that noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga indicates.

Industry observers note that still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot.

But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more vital than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”.

Recent findings suggest that during a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” claims neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.

Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.

Industry observers note that but the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.

Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy Robotics.

In a recent development, and connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.

In a recent development, medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.

“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit Bhatt.

Telesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra states, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.

It has been revealed that “Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.”.

If smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.

It has been revealed that in September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.

Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy Robotics.

In the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.

According to recent reports, the procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as swiftly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell notes. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy Robotics.

A few months after my visit, Remedy unveiled US $62 million in newly introduced funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”.

In a recent development, the steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga indicates they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.

These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person firm into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

10 stocks we like better than York Space Systems ›.

A wave of Wall Street price-target cuts following government contract delays sent York Space Systems (YSS +1.96%) tumbling 36.9% this week, according to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence.

York Space Systems stock changed hands at $3.65 as of the close on Friday, Nov. 20, down 36.9% from Friday, Nov. 13's close. Across those five sessions, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -3.70%) fell 5.1%, and the Nasdaq-100 was down 5.1%.

Analyst downgrades and price-target reductions hit the defense hardware provider throughout the week. Barclays cut its price target from $11 to $5, while JPMorgan lowered its target from $17 to $7. The reductions followed the company's third-quarter report, in which management revealed a $749.7 million goodwill impairment charge due to delayed government contract awards. The stock is down 92% (as of the close on Friday, Nov. 20) from its 52-week high of $44.54.

NYSE · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/20/26.

Recent findings suggest that york Space Systems manufactures small satellites and ground communications equipment for military, civil, and commercial space operators. It builds platforms like the Tranche 0 satellite line and Hydra MAX communications terminals used by national security agencies. The stock trades below $5, but the manufacturer generated $84.2 million in revenue last quarter from its spacecraft and ground hardware.

Recent findings suggest that management also declared plans to acquire Australian ground robotics maker Outlook Industries to expand into unmanned terrestrial defense systems. The deal expands York's total addressable market by $3.1 billion, but investors remained focused on near-term balance-sheet pressure. Wall Street's sharp price-target cuts invert the growth story, forcing investors to weigh a major impairment and defense contract delays against new expansion plans.

Sources indicate that york ended the quarter with $308.9 million in cash and short-term investments as of Sept. 30, 2026, against $179.8 million in total debt, including lease obligations. While the manufacturer holds a $14.9 billion pipeline of government opportunities, contract timing remains unpredictable. Investors will look to the closing of the Outlook acquisition and upcoming defense contract decisions in early 2027 to see if revenue growth recovers.

York Space Systems stock is available for a fraction of what it cost last spring when it was changing hands at north of $45.

Industry observers note that while York Space Systems claims it has a nearly $15 billion pipeline of government opportunities, there's no certainty that it will convert this to backlog -- and ultimately concrete sales. Take this, along with the fact that the company is burning through an increasing amount of cash -- operating cash flow through the first nine months of 2026 totaled $248.4 million compared to $88.2 million during the same period in 2025 -- and it seems that those seeking a compelling space stock opportunity now would be better off looking somewhere else.

It also comes with a flip-to-mute mic that makes you sound loud and clear, and its colorful design stands out. This is a budget headset that performs like a premium one.

Playing on Switch 2, the graphics don't look as good as on the other consoles, but you're sacrificing fidelity for the option to play on the go.

Industry observers note that this Super Mario Galaxy bundle brings the original games to Switch 2 in glorious HD. This game is also playable on Switch 1, though it lacks the graphical upgrades. This bundle is great for fans who want to relive the classic adventures, as well as for newcomers. At this price, it's hard to pass up!

If you're looking to upgrade your Nintendo Switch 2 setup, the PDP Afterglow is a great accessory to add to your wishlist. Its translucent design and customizable RGB lighting give the controller plenty of personality, with four preset lighting modes and adjustable brightness to help you find a look you like. There's more to it than flashy lights though. TMR thumbsticks are designed to deliver precise, responsive controls while reducing the risk of stick drift, and you also get built-in motion controls and two programmable back buttons.

There's even a dedicated C Button for quick access to Nintendo Switch 2's GameChat features. With wireless connectivity and up to 40 hours of battery life per charge, it's a handy alternative to your standard Joy-Con controllers. Plus, you can over 50% off right now, with PDP Afterglow now priced at just $24 at Amazon.

Sources indicate that A gaming headset doesn't have to cost a fortune, and the Turtle Beach Airlite Fit is a relatively simple option for Nintendo Switch players. It features 40mm speakers, a flip-to-mute microphone for chatting with friends and an onboard volume control.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that this shift changes how devices are designed.
  • This White Paper explains these challenges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cellular IoT has extended low-power connectivity to many remote places. Even so, about four-fifths of the earth’s surface remains outside the range of a base station. Non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by adding satellite access to the 5G standard. One modem can then connect through a satellite when no terrestrial cell is available.

Sources indicate that this shift changes how devices are designed. Satellites are in motion. Signals therefore face long propagation delays and changing Doppler shift. Link budgets are tight and device antennas are small. A device can pass static conformance tests and still fail on a real satellite link.

This White Paper explains these challenges. It also outlines the test conditions and measurements needed to evaluate synchronization, signaling, receiver performance, and link reliability.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When comparing free weights and gym machines, I am firmly on the side of free weights.
  • There are other benefits, too, like building stability, coordination, balance and range of motion, but I use certain gym machines like cables or leg presses, and I may start a beginner on certain machines until they feel more confident with the movements.
  • All of this is to say, there's one piece of equipment I avoid for core exercises, particularly sit-ups, because more often than not, I see people in the gym getting injured.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When comparing free weights and gym machines, I am firmly on the side of free weights. Equipment like dumbbells and kettlebells allows you to work both sides of your body independently, while using barbells means you can load heavy, working your core muscles harder to stabilize you without the help and support of a machine.

There are other benefits, too, like building stability, coordination, balance and range of motion, but I use certain gym machines like cables or leg presses, and I may start a beginner on certain machines until they feel more confident with the movements.

All of this is to say, there's one piece of equipment I avoid for core exercises, particularly sit-ups, because more often than not, I see people in the gym getting injured.

Read on for the full lowdown, and what to do instead.

Industry observers note that the GHD machine, or Glute Ham Developer as it was originally designed, can be used (and is commonly used) for sit-ups. The GHD sit-up is an intense sit-up variation used to improve core strength, stability and hip mobility, as it requires excessive and full range of motion as you lean back.

According to recent reports, although your hip flexors help power the torso upward, they shouldn't take over the exercise, which targets the abs running along the front of your stomach. The problem is, the excessive range of motion can load the lower back, and if you don't perform the exercise properly, with enough core engagement, or if you currently have a health condition (like high or low blood pressure), are pre- or post-natal, or have an injury, this exercise quickly becomes contraindicated.

For this reason, I skip the GHD machine for core exercises, especially for beginners, as repeated lumbar flexion and extension of the spine in an unsupported position offers more problems, in my opinion, than benefits.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Here's what I recommend instead.

You need a lot of power to drive your body to a sitting position, so the first thing I'll do is get someone on a pull-up bar for hanging leg raises or knee tucks. L-sits are also a great option for developing deep core strength while also targeting the hip flexors and grip strength.

Although your back is still unsupported, you're putting a lot less strain on your spine while still building strength in your upper body.

According to recent reports, if you're determined to use a GHD machine, I recommend relearning to brace your core using my five-minute bracing routine. Core engagement isn't just about squeezing your stomach hard or sucking your belly in; it's about gently bracing the abdomen and bearing down, as if someone is about to punch you in the gut. You'll also need to exhale as your body meets the most resistance, which means as you sit up in this case.

It has been revealed that finally, did you know your diaphragm is a core muscle? Breathing properly requires diaphragmatic breathing, which means directing your breath downward rather than out through your chest.

I strongly recommend spending some time activating your core and diaphragm first, and trying some pelvic tilts to get everything fired up beforehand while supporting your spine.

If possible, I would use dumbbells, Bosu trainers, resistance bands, kettlebells, or Swiss balls over going anywhere near the GHD machine.

Recent findings suggest that you can slowly overload the body as you get stronger, adding weight or volume as you develop core strength and stability. Bosu trainers test balance and stability, and kettlebells increase range of motion as you can move them more freely.

Sources indicate that free weights are also far more functional than many gym machines, as you teach your muscles to support you rather than relying on a piece of kit. This is extremely beneficial for your core, which in turn is better for your back health.

According to recent reports, movements that are functional should also feel natural, aiding everyday activities. Plus, you should feel like you have far more control.

Industry observers note that you put a lot of trust into the GHD when doing one of these sit-ups. Your entire body is held by the two rollers that clamp around your feet. It's not for everyone.

There's an extensive library of exercises that benefit your body more, and it's a great opportunity to experiment with what does and doesn't work for your body.

I would start with these 5 Pilates exercises and some lower abs workouts.

I also really rate endurance-focused core exercises that use isometric contraction, which means you hold tension in the working muscles without them lengthening or shortening. Examples include the hollow hold (pictured above) and plank variations.

I don't know many people who get away with zero pain using the GHD machine, and it might be a lack of core engagement, weakness in the stabilizing muscles, existing back pain, poor technique, or something as simple as body mechanics. For me, I just don't think it's worth the risk.

Give the tips above a try instead, and let us know how you get on by voting in the poll below!

Sam has written for various fitness brands and websites over the years and has experience across brands at Future, such as Live Science, Fit&Well, Coach, and T3.

Having coached at fitness studios like F45 and Virgin Active and taken on both 1:1 and group, Sam now primarily teaches outdoor bootcamps, bodyweight, and kettlebells.

She also coaches mobility and flexibility classes several times a week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that iOS 27.3 is right now in beta testing with developers and public beta customers. The enhancement includes multiple upcoming features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 ….

Sources indicate that 9to5Mac is supported by Sony: Score Sony’s ULT Field 1 Bluetooth speaker for 51% off. Powerful bass, room-filling sound, up to 12 hours of battery life, IP67 durability, stereo pairing support, and much more.

It has been revealed that as my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone customers sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:.

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

Recent findings suggest that the redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 people, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a latest Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

Industry observers note that for iPhone Duo owners, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left, making it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also brings a new face unlock feature to iPhone Duo. This is not full-fledged Face ID. Instead, Apple is using the front-facing camera on the iPhone Duo’s outer display to recognize you, then unlock the device. It doesn’t work for things like Apple Pay and passwords.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

Finally, iOS 27.3 includes a newly introduced option in the Settings app to have your iPhone Duo lock when closed. Once enabled, your iPhone Duo will lock when you fold it, rather than transition content from the inner display to the outer display.

Sources indicate that when it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The patch also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many newly introduced capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:.

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so owners can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

It has been revealed that there are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

It has been revealed that with iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test upcoming ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:.

Industry observers note that today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to latest languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

According to recent reports, iOS 27.3 also introduces usage limits on select Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features. The limits apply to things like:.

Industry observers note that you can unlock higher usage limits with an eligible iCloud+ plan, starting at $2.99 per month. If you hit your usage limit, basic Siri requests will still work. That includes things like setting timers and alarms.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:.

Industry observers note that iOS 27.3 is a major revision to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

Industry observers note that iOS 27.3 also adds a newly introduced Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Recent findings suggest that for Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a latest “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The enhancement also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

There are two key changes to the Apple TV app in iOS 27.3. First, the update introduces video podcasts in the TV app. You can now watch your favorite video podcasts in the TV app, and sync your playback progress between the TV app and the Podcasts app.

Recent findings suggest that second, iOS 27.3 adds vertical video to the TV app. The app now includes a new “Explore Clip Collections” section where you can browse clips from Apple TV content in a TikTok-style design.

#131148. Latest Update: Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Apple’s ‘just works’ approach is great, but goes a little too far

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple.
  • Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….
  • Industry observers note that macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that “It just works” is one of the phrases most commonly associated with Apple. Interestingly, it appears to have been coined by the tech giant’s customers and then used by reviewers before it was later picked up by Steve Jobs.

Of course, it’s now commonly used ironically when Apple products don’t do what they are supposed to (Apple Home, I’m looking at you), but I do think that it’s absolutely the right philosophy and goal – most of the time ….

Industry observers note that macworld referenced an Apple brochure from 1996 entitled “Why do people prefer Macintosh?” This is a collection of testimonials from customers, a number of whom use the “it just works” phrasing. It was subsequently used by a number of reviewers. The earliest example I can find of Steve Jobs adopting it was in 1999, when discussing the rollout of FireWire to the Mac in the PowerMac G3.

Industry observers note that it’s hot-pluggable. You don’t have to turn your computer off to connect and disconnect peripherals, you can just plug them right in. Again, the drivers are dynamically loaded. There are no terminators and there are no switches. It just works.

(If you have a link to any earlier example, please do let me know in the comments.).

According to recent reports, I’m a significant fan of the philosophy. Most of the time, owners should just be able to get on with the tasks they want to execute without having to worry about the technology. The tech that makes it all possible should sit there quietly in the background.

However, there are cases where I think Apple takes this approach a little too far, and where tech-savvy customers at least would like a little more transparency and control.

Sources indicate that airPods firmware updates are a good example. Back in September, there was quite a significant revision in the form of custom EQ. It’s a rather basic version, but still a feature many had wanted for a long time. Instead of being able to manually trigger the update, people had to wait until it “just worked.”.

Sources indicate that apple’s support document has a how-to guide that is essentially an outline of the conditions required to permit an revision, and an instruction to simply wait until it happens. Which you will only know by repeatedly checking.

Make sure your AirPods are connected via Bluetooth to your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Connect your charging case to a power source. Put your AirPods in their charging case and close the lid. Keep the lid of the charging case closed, and keep your AirPods in Bluetooth range of your iPhone, iPad or Mac. Wait at least 30 minutes for the firmware to be updated. Check the firmware version again.

In a recent development, another example, and one I’ve complained about before, is that there is no way to manually trigger an iCloud document sync, nor any progress indicator when it does finally happen. In the best of cases, it takes seconds; in the worst, many hours. And again, the only way to find out is to repeatedly check.

Sources indicate that it’s the same story when shooting a video on your iPhone. Will it still be there an hour later, available to instantly edit and view? Maybe, or maybe it will have been offloaded to the cloud, requiring it to be downloaded before you can do anything with it – while a video you shot months earlier is still stored locally on the device! You can, of course, switch off optimization altogether, but if you choose to use it, you get no control over it. I want a setting that allows me to do things like specify local retention of all photos and videos taken within the past fortnight.

Will that video be available in the Mac Photos app when you check half an hour later? Maybe, maybe not. You can click the Sync Now button as many times as you like, and it will apparently have no effect, claiming it’s up to date despite the video being entirely absent. It will be there when it’s there.

Industry observers note that once it is in the Photos app on your Mac, it’s a similar story when exporting it to a folder. You can drag and drop the video into the folder, and this time you are manually triggering the transfer (yay!), but there will be absolutely no visual indication that it is in progress. No grayed-out icon, no progress bar, nothing. So far as the user interface is concerned, it appears that your drag and drop had no effect – until the video file finally appears.

Recent findings suggest that I think with all of these things and more, Apple needs to offer options. Yes, most non-tech people may be perfectly happy to just wait until things happen, but there ought to be a standard way to trigger things that presently happen in their own sweet time, as well as progress indicators and confirmation that a process is complete.

It has been revealed that is this an ecosystem-wide improvement you’d like to see? Please share your thoughts in the comments and add any frustrating examples of your own.
